description_full: NewMarket Corporation, through its subsidiaries, primarily engages in the manufacture and sale of petroleum additives. It offers lubricant additives for use in various vehicle and industrial applications, including engine oils, transmission fluids, off-road powertrain and hydraulic systems, gear oils, hydraulic oils, turbine oils, and other applications where metal-to-metal moving parts are utilized; engine oil additives designed for passenger cars, motorcycles, on and off-road heavy duty commercial equipment, locomotives, and engines in ocean-going vessels; driveline additives designed for products, such as transmission fluids, axle fluids, and off-road powertrain fluids; and industrial additives designed for products for industrial applications consisting of hydraulic fluids, greases, industrial gear fluids, and industrial specialty applications comprising turbine oils. The company also provides fuel additives that are used to enhance the oil refining process and the performance of gasoline, diesel, biofuels, and other fuels to industry, government, original equipment manufacturers, and individual customers. In addition, it engages in the marketing of antiknock compounds, as well as contracted manufacturing and related services; and owns and manages a real property in Virginia. The company operates in North America, Latin America, the Asia Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, India, and internationally. NewMarket Corporation was founded in 1887 and is headquartered in Richmond, Virginia.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 2K people. Revenue per employee of $1.3M ranks in the top quartile among Basic Materials peers. Each employee generates $240K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (4/10).
financial_summary: NewMarket Corp is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $6.5B market cap on $2.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -0% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 18% against a 8% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 29%.

The business throws off $491M in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.36× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 14× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 19% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Above-average short interest at 8.2% of float
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 11% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
20 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Basic Materials peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood

sect: Its 20% operating margin runs 11pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 16% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 26% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 28% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 33% and a beta of 0.63, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $107.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 31% in the 2020 crash, 20% in the 2022 bear market and 73% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 8% below its DCF fair value of $771, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 8%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $617 to $971 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: P/FCF 13.3 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 17% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 3.7% annual cash-flow growth, 1pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.28).
It runs a 29% gross margin and converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow, or 11% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.36x.
ROE of 24% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
It spends 4.8% of revenue on R&D.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.2x net debt to EBITDA ($77.6M of cash against $883.4M of debt), with interest covered 13.7x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.5, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -0.5% over 3 years, 6.3% over 5 years and 2.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 20.8% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (2.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 19.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 66%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (1 purchase, net $248K bought).
It returns 2.8% a year to shareholders (1.2% in buybacks and 1.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 20 consecutive years, raising it 4.9% a year over the last five.
people: With about 2,050 employees, each generates about $1.3M of revenue, 2.1x the Basic Materials median, and revenue has grown 2.8% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $240K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.1M (2x revenue per employee).
